outcome: Since 26 January 2024 OpenAI has posted (10 July 2026) a claimed proof of the full conjecture, credited in its own material to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra run with up to 64 subagents; two expositions by named specialists and a Lean 4 development (openai/cdc-lean) accompany it, but I found no journal acceptance as of 11 October 2026, and a second, independent 2026 claim of the full result (Kintali, arXiv:2607.14140) has no engagement I could find.
problem_asks: (1) For every bridgeless graph G: read as every finite bridgeless graph. The statement does not say whether loops or parallel edges count as 'graph'; the literature varies (Oum's exposition allows parallel edges and loops; the Lean development is for loopless multigraphs; Wikipedia says 'finite bridgeless undirected graph'). (2) There exists a family (a list, so repeated cycles are allowed) of cycles of G. (3) Each edge of G lies in exactly two members of that family; 'includes each edge twice' is read as exactly twice, following the standard statement (Wikipedia: 'each edge belongs to exactly two cycles'). Not asked by the bullet and so not required: a cycle count or cycle length bound, containment of a prescribed cycle (Goddyn's stronger conjecture), or the cubic case (a reduction, not a restriction).

events.what_happened: Ali Ghassab, 'On The Cycle Double Cover Problem', arXiv:1201.5203. The abstract claims a proof of the conjecture via Kuratowski-minor properties and says 'As a result, the cycle double cover conjecture has been concluded.' Also claims Goddyn's conjecture. Withdrawn: v4 (1 Mar 2022) comment reads 'One of the basic lemma of the paper is false, and the following results have not been proved'.
events.revisions: v1 25 Jan 2012; v2 5 Mar 2012; v3 6 Mar 2012; v4 1 Mar 2022 (withdrawn, 1 KB).
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture (all bridgeless graphs) and Goddyn's stronger form. Withdrawn, so the claim does not stand.
events.remains: Nothing, on the author's claim; the claim was withdrawn.
events.doubts: Withdrawn by the author; the comment names a false basic lemma. I did not read the full text.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true (affirmative), withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Alexander Souza, 'A Constructive Proof of the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture', arXiv:1202.0569. Abstract: 'In this paper, we settle the conjecture in the affirmative.' Withdrawn in v2 (7 Feb 2012): 'Due to a flaw in Lemma 9, the paper has been withdrawn'. Open Problem Garden comment of 7 Feb 2012 (Andrew King) says 'there is an unresolved problem with Lemma 9' and that 'the Petersen graph is a counterexample to Theorem 2', unless the commenter is mistaken.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture by a constructive polynomial-time algorithm. Withdrawn.
events.remains: Nothing, on the author's claim; withdrawn.
events.directly_checkable: The Petersen graph is named in an Open Problem Garden comment as a possible counterexample to Theorem 2 (the commenter flags they may be mistaken). I did not check this.
events.doubts: Withdrawn for a flaw in Lemma 9. Open Problem Garden comment alleges a counterexample to Theorem 2 (unverified, and the commenter hedges).

withdrawn.what: Whole paper withdrawn for a flaw in Lemma 9

events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true (affirmative), withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Paul Clarke, 'Cycle Double Cover Conjecture', arXiv:1401.0908. Claims a proof by induction on the number of edges, adding an edge to a bridgeless graph and reforming the cover. Withdrawn in v2 (26 Mar 2014) and v3 (6 Apr 2014): 'due to a critical error in the proof of theorem 3', thanking P. Seymour.

events.remains: Nothing, on the author's claim; withdrawn.

withdrawn.what: Withdrawn for a critical error in the proof of theorem 3 (first withdrawal v2, 26 Mar 2014; v3 6 Apr 2014 also withdrawn)

events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true (affirmative), withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Mary Radcliffe, 'A proof of the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture', arXiv:1510.02075. Abstract: 'We here present a proof that every bridgeless cubic graph has a cycle double cover', via cycles in the line graph; also claims that for cubic graphs every cycle of a bridgeless graph lies in some cover (Goddyn's strengthening). General case follows only via Jaeger's reduction to cubic graphs. Comment on v2: 'an error in Subcase 2.2.1(a) was pointed out by Peter Nelson and Jim Geelan [sic] and verified by Arthur Hoffman-Ostenhof'; the author is 'working to resolve it'.
events.revisions: v1 7 Oct 2015; v2 9 Oct 2015 (current when I read it; the comment on v2 acknowledges the error).
events.delivers: Cubic case of the conjecture (every bridgeless cubic graph). The general case follows only through Jaeger's reduction, which the abstract states. The Goddyn-type cycle-containment statement is for cubic graphs only.
events.remains: The non-cubic case is not proved here; the cubic case is claimed, with an acknowledged unfixed error in a subcase.

checked_by.who: Peter Nelson and Jim Geelen (spelt 'Jim Geelan' in the comment) and Arthur Hoffman-Ostenhof
checked_by.qualification: Named in the author's own comment as having found and verified an error
checked_by.what_they_did: Found an error in Subcase 2.2.1(a) (Nelson, Geelen); verified it (Hoffman-Ostenhof); per the comment

events.doubts: Acknowledged error in Subcase 2.2.1(a) per the v2 comment; the comment says the author was working on a fix, and I found no later version in my checks.
events.direction: Claims the cubic case of the conjecture (affirmative for cubic graphs); general case only via reduction.

events.what_happened: Bin Shen, 'Weak embedding theorem and a proof of cycle double cover of bridgeless graphs', arXiv:1712.06953. Abstract: 'In this article, we give a positive answer to the cycle double cover conjecture.' Single version; 22 pages, 1 figure.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture. Method and structure not checked by me (abstract and front matter only).
events.doubts: No public engagement found; single version; no journal listed in my checks.

events.what_happened: A. Alipour and A. Tayebi (arXiv author order), 'A Simple Proof for the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture', arXiv:1811.08719. Abstract: 'In this paper, we prove the cycle double cover conjecture'; proves Goddyn's stronger conjecture (every cycle of G is in some cover) as the route. Single version; comment: 'we prove the Goddyn's conjecture. Thus, we prove the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture'.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture, via the stronger cycle-containment statement (Goddyn). Method not checked by me.
events.doubts: No journal and no public engagement found; single version. The route through a stronger statement (Goddyn) is itself a claim that would need checking; Radcliffe's cubic-case claim is the closest prior attempt on that statement.
events.direction: Claims the conjecture is true (affirmative), via Goddyn's stronger form.

events.what_happened: Lingsheng Shi and Zhang Zhang, 'Signed cycle double covers', Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 25(4) (2018), P4.63, DOI 10.37236/6760. Proves that every bridgeless graph has a signed cycle double cover (a signed analogue; the abstract calls it 'a weak version of this conjecture'). It does not claim the unsigned conjecture.
events.revisions: Journal publication 21 Dec 2018. An earlier arXiv or preprint version was not found. A received date of 20 Jan 2017 appears in a search summary only and is unverified.
events.delivers: A signed analogue: every bridgeless graph has a signed cycle double cover. Different question from the unsigned bullet; the abstract says it is a weaker statement, and it relates to Tutte flow conjectures and the shortest cycle cover conjecture.
events.remains: The unsigned conjecture: all of problem_asks.

checked_by.who: Electronic Journal of Combinatorics (refereeing process not visible on the page)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper; the page lists only the publication date

events.direction: Proves a weaker, signed analogue; does not claim the unsigned conjecture.

events.what_happened: Radek Hušek and Robert Šámal, 'Counting Circuit Double Covers', arXiv:2303.10615 (2023; revised Sept 2024 per a search summary). Conjectures that every bridgeless cubic graph has at least 2^(n/2-1) circuit double covers, shows an infinite family where it is tight, and gives lower bounds for surface-embedded and planar graphs. Published in the Journal of Graph Theory 2025 (vol. 108, no. 2) per a search snippet.
events.revisions: arXiv 2303 identifier (2023); revised Sept 2024 per a search summary; journal JGT 2025 per a search snippet (neither opened).
events.delivers: A counting question (how many circuit double covers), not whether one exists. Conjectured lower bound is for bridgeless cubic graphs; the proven bounds are for subclasses. Does not settle the existence question asked by the bullet.
events.remains: All of problem_asks; this is a different question (counting), per the scope rule.
events.direction: Neighbouring counting question; no direction on the bullet.

events.what_happened: Edita Máčajová, Giuseppe Mazzuoccolo and Gloria Tabarelli, Ars Mathematica Contemporanea paper on cycle-separating cuts in a smallest counterexample to the cycle double cover conjecture (and Berge-Fulkerson). For a cycle-separating 4-cut, the admissible covers along the dangling edges are determined uniquely among more than 219 a priori possibilities. Received 12 June 2024 per the journal PDF (search snippet). Publication year is inconsistent across sources: Iris record says 2025, PDF says online 21 Jan 2026.
events.revisions: Received 12 June 2024; accepted 6 March 2025; online 21 January 2026 (per the PDF, search snippet only). The earlier arXiv or preprint date was not checked.
events.delivers: Structural restriction on a hypothetical smallest counterexample (a 4-cut analysis). Does not produce a counterexample and does not prove the conjecture.
events.direction: Structural reduction for a hypothetical counterexample; neither confirms nor refutes the conjecture. Treats the conjecture as open.

events.what_happened: Jens Walter Fischer, 'The cycle double cover conjecture from the perspective of percolation theory on iterated line graphs', arXiv:2307.06649 (earlier version titled 'Constructive proof of the cycle double cover conjecture', per a search summary). Abstract opens 'We prove the conjecture', but the labelling result is stated for simple bridgeless triangle-free cubic graphs. Abstract: lift walks and cycles to open and closed edges on the line graph of the line graph; the labelling of double walk covers projects to a double cycle cover when G is a simple bridgeless triangle-free cubic graph.
events.revisions: v1 13 Jul 2023; v2 16 Jul 2023; v3 5 Dec 2024; v4 2 Jan 2025; v5 4 Mar 2025 (current when I read it). v4 comment: 'adding details/completeness for the monotonicity argument, minor updates regarding discovered typos'.
events.delivers: Explicit labelling result for simple bridgeless triangle-free cubic graphs. The abstract claims the full conjecture, and the step from the triangle-free cubic class to all graphs (by edge-contraction and degree-3 expansion arguments, per a search summary) is what carries the claim. I did not verify that step.
events.remains: If the reduction from the triangle-free cubic class to all bridgeless graphs holds, nothing; otherwise the general case.
events.doubts: Explicit result covers only simple bridgeless triangle-free cubic graphs; the general claim depends on a reduction I did not check. No engagement found; no journal listed in my checks.
events.direction: Claims the full conjecture; the explicit labelling is restricted to a cubic subclass.

events.what_happened: Cun-Quan Zhang, 'Some Early Results by Tutte Regarding the Cycle Double Cover Conjecture in 1948', arXiv:2609.10618 (8 Sep 2026). Argues that the problem is older than the press '50-year-old' description: a 1987 letter from Tutte to Fleischner shows it has been open 'for at least 80 years', and two early results appear in a Tutte 1949 publication (abstract; the title says 1948). Mentions OpenAI's announcement but does not assess the proof.
events.delivers: History only. Establishes no mathematical result on the conjecture and no status change.
events.direction: None on the conjecture's truth; historical dating only.

events.what_happened: Babak Ghanbari and Robert Šámal, 'Approximate cycle double cover', arXiv:2511.07285 (10 Nov 2025). Recasts the conjecture as: bridgeless cubic graphs have an embedding with no singular edge (a singular edge is visited twice by one face boundary). Proves nontrivial upper bounds on the minimum number of singular edges in an embedding of a cubic graph, with efficient algorithms. Preliminary version at IWOCA 2024 (LNCS 14764) per the bibliography (search snippet).
events.revisions: v1 10 Nov 2025 only (per arXiv listing); IWOCA 2024 preliminary version per search snippet.
events.delivers: Upper bounds on singular edges in embeddings (an equivalent reformulation of the conjecture per the abstract). Gives no embedding with zero singular edges, so it does not settle the conjecture. The exact bounds are not in the abstract.
events.direction: Approximation toward an equivalent embedding form; neither confirms nor refutes.

events.what_happened: Shiva Kintali, 'Three-Bit Flows and Cycle Covers. Part I', arXiv:2607.14140 (13 Jul 2026, math.CO). Abstract: uses Seymour and Tutte flow theorems to assign local labels at each vertex; encodes agreement across edges as a binary system and argues solvability by 'an inconsistency certificate, a local tester-parity identity, and a global double count'; traces cycle components from compatible labels; claims 'proving that every finite bridgeless multigraph has a cycle double cover, proving the cycle double cover conjecture'. The title says 'Part I'; I found no Part II.
events.revisions: v1 13 Jul 2026 only, as of my read.
events.delivers: Claims the full conjecture for finite bridgeless multigraphs (loops not mentioned in the abstract as read). Method is a binary-system solvability argument; I read the abstract only.
events.doubts: Abstract compresses the key solvability step into one sentence, and the full paper was not read. No engagement found in my searches; no citing work found. It uses the same kind of linear system as the OpenAI argument (per Hušek and Šámal's abstract, which says the OpenAI proof uses 'the same system of linear equations'), so the two are not fully independent in method, although the abstract describes different inputs (Seymour and Tutte flow theorems).

events.what_happened: OpenAI announced on 10 July 2026 a proof of the full cycle double cover conjecture, 'in just under one hour', credited to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra run with up to 64 concurrent subagents. OpenAI posted a three-page proof PDF and a prompt PDF on its CDN (cdn.openai.com/pdf/04d1d1e4-.../cdc_proof.pdf and .../cdc_prompt.pdf), and a Lean 4 development at github.com/openai/cdc-lean (8 commits on main, undated on the page). OpenAI researcher Ethan Knight announced it on X (Scientific American; Wikipedia). Announcement dates in secondary sources vary (10, 11 or 12 July). I could not open the PDFs, so their wording comes from secondary reports, the Lean code, and the arXiv expositions.
events.revisions: No revision found. The OpenAI PDFs were not readable with my tools, so I could not check whether they were revised. Lean repository: 8 commits on main, dates not visible.
events.delivers: Claims that every bridgeless graph has a cycle double cover: the full conjecture. Scope differs by source: 'every finite bridgeless undirected graph' (Wikipedia, and per a search summary of the PDF) versus 'every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph' (the Lean README and the Breakthrough Tracker). The Lean statement is for loopless multigraphs. The cubic case is an internal reduction (Jaeger), not a restriction of the claim.
events.remains: Nothing of problem_asks, if the claim is correct. The claim is unrefereed (see doubts).

checked_by.qualification: Matroid and graph-connectivity researcher (per a university profile seen in search results, not opened: PhD Hamburg 2015; Birmingham)

The post does not give the details of the check in the portion I read.

Restates the argument with a cubic reduction (Prop. 3), Fleischner's splitting lemma, Nash-Williams-Tutte, a three-spanning-tree lemma and a linear-algebra completion. No explicit verdict found in the text I read.

checked_by.who: Thomas Bloom (per Wikipedia and AIWeekly; not read at source)

Per AIWeekly: praised the proof as surprisingly elementary but criticised the lack of citations to prior work. The original posts were not reached.

machine_checked.note: Text scan of the 15 files in CDCLean/ that I could read (Audit, Basic, CubicBridge, CubicLabeling, CubicTheorem, CycleDecomposition, EvenCover, Expansion, FlowCount, GeneralGraph, JaegerKilpatrick, Main, NashWilliams, PathCut, SixFlow): no sorry, admit, axiom, opaque, native_decide or unsafe. I did not compile the project or run Audit.lean; the expected output (only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) is stated in the file, not shown. The text scan was read by a tool, not by grep. The listing said 'View all files', so there may be files I did not see. Headline theorem: cycleDoubleCover_of_bridgeless, 'Every finite bridgeless graph has a cycle double cover', for FiniteGraph with loopless. The Jaeger-Kilpatrick Z_2^3 eight-flow theorem (JaegerKilpatrick.lean) is proved, not assumed; NashWilliams.lean proves nashWilliamsTutte; PathCut.lean proves the path/cut dichotomy. The file CubicTheorem.lean has conditional variants that take Seymour's six-flow as a hypothesis, and cycleDoubleCover_of_sixFlow is labelled a conditional variant; the unconditional route does not use them, per the README.

events.directly_checkable: The three-page proof (not readable with my tools) and the Lean development at github.com/openai/cdc-lean. The Lean statement is checkable by a specialist for correspondence with the bullet's wording.
events.doubts: (1) No journal acceptance or named referee report found; MathWorld, updated 2 Oct 2026, says the claim had 'not yet appeared in a refereed publication'. (2) I could not read the proof PDF, so I checked no step of the proof informally; the Oum and Geelen expositions are the only step-level readings I saw, and both reproduce the argument rather than check it independently. (3) The Lean check is of the encoded statement: Breakthrough Tracker says specialists must still assess correspondence with the accepted conjecture. (4) Scope differs by source (loops, multigraphs, 'finite'). (5) Timing conflicts: announced 'in just under one hour' versus a prompt that says 'Spend at least 8 hours on this' (Kingy audit calls this unresolved). (6) Bloom reportedly criticised the lack of citations to prior work (including Bermond-Jackson-Jaeger 1983 for the flow approach). (7) The Lean development's scope and the author's claim of 'machine-verified' status are not the same thing; one search summary calls it 'machine-verified', which is an overstatement relative to the other sources. (8) Not doubts about the proof per se: Alon's 'the proof is short' and Sutherland's comments (Scientific American) are reactions, not checks.
events.direction: Affirmative: claims the conjecture is true for every bridgeless graph in the scope above. Produces no counterexample.

systems.basis_quote: The proof in this note is entirely due to GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra and the writeup with Codex.

The Kingy audit says the timing tension is unresolved. No token or dollar figure was found in the sources I read.

events.what_happened: Sang-il Oum, 'A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture by OpenAI: An exposition', arXiv:2607.16356 (v1 17 Jul 2026; v2 23 Jul; v3 1 Aug 2026). Presents OpenAI's proof 'with slight modifications intended to make it more accessible'. Theorem 1: 'Every bridgeless graph has a cycle double cover', allowing parallel edges and loops in its graphs (arXiv HTML). Reduction to cubic 3-edge-connected graphs (Prop. 3, via Fleischner's splitting lemma and Nash-Williams-Tutte); proves the 3-edge-connected Z_2^3 nowhere-zero flow case (Lemma 8, 'weaker'); linear-algebra criterion (Lemma 12: column space = orthogonal complement of left null space); cubic case completes it. Section 9 consequences: 'Every bridgeless graph has an 8-cycle double cover' (9.2), '7-cycle 4-cover' (9.4), matroid consequence via Jamshy and Tarsi (9.5).
events.revisions: v1 17 Jul 2026 (11 KB); v2 23 Jul 2026 (11 KB); v3 1 Aug 2026 (13 KB; current when I read it). The arXiv comments field reads '10 pages; Adding subsections on small cycle double cover conjecture (suggested by Adrian Bondy) and implications to matroids, due to Jamshy and Tarsi'; the version it refers to is not stated.
events.delivers: Restates OpenAI's argument for every bridgeless graph (with the scope above). No new independent resolution. Adds claimed consequences: an 8-cycle double cover for every bridgeless graph (stronger than the bullet, and it implies it); a 7-cycle 4-cover; a matroid reformulation. The small-cycle-double-cover corollary (9.1) is attributed to Lai, Yu and Zhang.
events.remains: Nothing of problem_asks beyond what the OpenAI argument claims; this is an exposition, not a separate check.

checked_by.qualification: Combinatorialist; an IBS seminar of 16 Jul 2026 on the proof (IBS page)
checked_by.what_they_did: Digested rewrite of the OpenAI proof; no verdict on correctness stated in the text I read

events.doubts: Modifications are described only in general terms in the text I read ('the choice of values at each edge is now symmetric'; linear algebra done 'without using dual vector spaces'). The exposition is not an independent check of OpenAI's argument.
people: Vahan Mkrtchyan and Adrian Bondy (thanked in acknowledgements)

events.what_happened: Jim Geelen, 'OpenAI's proof of the Cycle Double Cover Theorem', arXiv:2607.15399 (v1 16 Jul 2026, 3 pages). Expository notes: 'The following notes are my attempt to clarify, to myself, the OpenAI proof'. States that 'OpenAI uses linear algebra to construct an edge-bicolouring from a nowhere-zero F_2^3-flow', with Jaeger's theorem that every bridgeless graph admits such a flow, and the reduction to cubic graphs ('It suffices to prove the Cycle Double Cover Theorem for cubic graphs'). References 'OpenAI, A proof of the cycle double cover conjecture, July 2026'.
events.revisions: v1 16 Jul 2026 only, as of my read.
events.delivers: Restates OpenAI's argument for all bridgeless graphs (via the cubic reduction). No new result, per its own statement.
events.remains: Nothing of problem_asks beyond what the OpenAI argument claims.

checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote notes to understand the OpenAI argument; states it 'offers no new insights'. Does not state a verdict on correctness in the text I read.

events.what_happened: Johannes Carmesin's Matroid Union post (21 Jul 2026) says the OpenAI proof 'has already been formalised independently several times in Lean 4', listing: a formalisation of the core argument by Krystal Guo; one by Carmesin, Vaibhav Bajpai and Utku Okur; and one by OpenAI. I found no repository, size or axiom audit for the Guo or Bajpai-Okur-Carmesin formalisations in my searches, and the post gives none.
events.delivers: Claimed formalisations of the theorem. Not verified: no link, size or axiom audit found. Carmesin says the formal checks confirm the statement 'every bridgeless multigraph G can be embedded in a pseudosurface in such a way that every face is a disc' (from a search summary; not confirmed in the post text I read).
events.remains: Unknown until the formalisations are located.
events.doubts: Claims of formalisations by named people with no links found in my searches. The 'pseudosurface' statement comes from a search summary and is not confirmed in the post text I read.

events.what_happened: Arshia Soltani Moakhar, Iman Gholami, Max Springer, Mahdi JafariRaviz and MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi, 'Beyond the Library: An Agentic Framework for Autoformalizing Research Mathematics', arXiv:2606.31134. Among seven research manuscripts formalised, it reports a 'sorry-free formalization in 5,713 lines of Lean code' of the OpenAI cycle double cover manuscript ('This recent graph-theory manuscript proves that every finite bridgeless undirected graph has a cycle double cover'). Its 'final axiom audit contains exactly three citation-backed classical inputs': Fleischner's splitting lemma, the Nash-Williams-Tutte spanning-tree packing theorem, and Veblen's even-graph cycle decomposition; 'Apart from these inputs, the development uses only Lean's standard kernel axioms.' Credits the manuscript to 'OpenAI (2026)' ('two recent OpenAI manuscripts').
events.revisions: v1 submitted 30 Jun 2026 (before OpenAI's 10 July announcement, so it cannot cite the OpenAI manuscript); v3 last revised 5 Aug 2026 (the version I read, which cites OpenAI). Whether v1 or v2 carries the CDC formalisation was not checked. The first version carrying it is between 10 Jul and 5 Aug 2026; the date field is therefore left null.
events.delivers: A formal (Lean 4) development of the OpenAI manuscript's theorem. Per the authors, sorry-free, but conditional on three cited classical inputs that appear in its axiom audit, so it is not axiom-free. This is formalisation of an argument already given, not a new mathematical argument.
events.remains: Nothing of problem_asks; the formal result depends on three named classical inputs (Fleischner's splitting lemma, Nash-Williams-Tutte, Veblen's cycle decomposition) cited rather than proved in that development.

machine_checked.note: The authors' own claim, from the arXiv HTML (v3). I did not find the repository or check the code. The audit's three inputs are cited, not proved, in that development.

events.doubts: Author claim of 'sorry-free' with three cited inputs, read via a tool from the arXiv HTML; the repository was not located. The authors' pipeline is driven by Claude Code (see ai); whether this affects the formal proof is for the judging pass.
events.direction: Formal confirmation of the OpenAI claim (conditional on three cited inputs).

ai.disclosed_cost: For the cycle double cover run only (Appendix B, 'Our cost'): 516 million total tokens and $438.31 API-equivalent, from Claude Code logs (deduplicated from 8,514 stored records to 3,804 distinct messages); wall-clock 45.7 hours. The unit-distance run is separate (2.78 billion tokens, $2,480.64).

events.what_happened: Radek Hušek and Robert Šámal, 'Exponentially Many Circuit Double Covers', arXiv:2607.24724 (27 Jul 2026). Proves the 2^(n/2-1) lower bound (their own 2023 conjecture) for 2-edge-connected 3-edge-colourable cubic graphs on n vertices, and a weaker exponential bound for 3-edge-connected cubic graphs of girth at least 16; uses 'the same system of linear equations used by OpenAI in their proof', with a combinatorial interpretation. Also a planarity characterisation and a 5-cycle double cover flow condition.
events.delivers: Counting bounds for a subclass (3-edge-colourable cubic graphs), not the existence question for all bridgeless graphs. The abstract says the OpenAI result is 'a separate statement' and does not assess it.
events.remains: All of problem_asks (the counting bound is a different question and covers only a subclass).
events.direction: Neighbouring counting results; neither confirms nor refutes the conjecture.

disputes.summary: Bloom reportedly criticised the OpenAI paper for not citing prior work, and noted that using nowhere-zero flows on cubic graphs for this problem goes back to Bermond, Jackson and Jaeger (1983). The OpenAI credit is thus contested on the citation point. Bloom's remarks are secondhand (Wikipedia; AIWeekly); the original posts were not reached.

Model naming differs across sources: 'GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra' (OpenAI and most press), 'GPT 5.6' (Oum's exposition), 'gpt-5.6-sol' with Ultra as a multi-agent setting (Kingy audit). The Codex write-up credit is reported only in secondary sources. The exact OpenAI wording could not be checked against the PDF.

Announcement date of the OpenAI claim is reported as 10 July 2026 (Wikipedia, IBS seminar page), 11 July (some secondary coverage; Pegg's Wolfram post dated 11 July) and 12 July (Odaily, for Knight's X post). I use 10 July, the date the PDFs were released per the Wikipedia article and the IBS page.

Scope of the OpenAI claim differs by source: 'every finite bridgeless undirected graph' (Wikipedia; search summary of the PDF) and 'every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph' (Lean README and Breakthrough Tracker). Oum's exposition states Theorem 1 for all bridgeless graphs and says its graphs allow parallel edges and loops. This matters for whether loops are in scope of the bullet.

The problem's age: press calls it a '50-year-old' problem; Cun-Quan Zhang argues from a 1987 Tutte-to-Fleischner letter that it has been open 'for at least 80 years', citing early Tutte results from 1948/1949. This is a dispute about dating, not about status.
Two 2026 claims of the full conjecture by different authors and methods (OpenAI, 10 Jul 2026; Kintali, 13 Jul 2026). No source I found compares them.

summary: Since January 2024 the one serious development is OpenAI's claimed proof of the full conjecture, posted 10 July 2026 and credited in OpenAI's own material to GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra run with up to 64 subagents. It comes with a prompt PDF and a Lean 4 development (openai/cdc-lean). I could not open OpenAI's PDFs with my tools, so the attribution sentence 'The proof in this note is entirely due to GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra and the writeup with Codex' is only as reported by a search summary and AIWeekly, and the proof's wording and the prompt are from secondary coverage. What I could read: Oum's arXiv exposition (v3, 1 Aug 2026) states 'The proof presented in this note is due to GPT 5.6 announced by OpenAI' and says parts of his revision were done with GPT 5.6 under his guidance; Geelen's notes (16 Jul 2026) restate the argument and say they add no new insights; Carmesin's Matroid Union post (21 Jul 2026) says 'yes, the proof is correct'. Scientific American quotes Noga Alon ('It is a well-known conjecture'; 'the proof is short'), which is a reaction, not a check. For the Lean development I read all 15 visible files in openai/cdc-lean and found no sorry, admit, axiom, opaque, native_decide or unsafe; the headline theorem is for loopless multigraphs, uses a proved Z_2^3 eight-flow theorem (JaegerKilpatrick.lean) and a proved Nash-Williams-Tutte (NashWilliams.lean), and does not use the conditional Seymour six-flow variant. I did not compile it, and the authors' Audit.lean output (expected: only propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound) is not shown. A second, independent Lean development (Soltani Moakhar et al., arXiv:2606.31134) reports a sorry-free 5,713-line formalisation of the manuscript but cites three classical inputs (Fleischner's splitting lemma, Nash-Williams-Tutte, Veblen's cycle decomposition) in its axiom audit, so it is sorry-free but not axiom-free; that run cost 516 million tokens and $438.31 in Claude Code logs. Against acceptance: no journal publication or named referee report found (MathWorld, updated 2 Oct 2026: 'had not yet appeared in a refereed publication'; Breakthrough Tracker: 'Peer reviewed: No'); the sources disagree on the announcement date, the model naming, and the scope (loops, multigraphs, 'finite'); the prompt's 'at least 8 hours' conflicts with 'just under one hour'; Bloom reportedly criticised the lack of citations to prior work. A separate 2026 preprint by Kintali (arXiv:2607.14140, 13 Jul 2026) also claims the full result by a different route; I found no engagement with it. Earlier full-conjecture claims were withdrawn (Ghassab 2012; Souza 2012; Clarke 2014), and Radcliffe (2015, cubic case) carries an acknowledged error in a subcase with no fix I could find; Shen (2017), Tayebi and Alipour (2018) and Fischer (2023, whose explicit labelling is restricted to triangle-free cubic graphs) have had no visible uptake. Neighbouring work (signed covers 2018; counting covers 2023 and 2026; approximate covers 2025; cut structure of a smallest counterexample 2024/26) is a different question and settles nothing here. No counterexample or exhibited object has been claimed. AI involvement appears only in the 2026 events: the OpenAI claim (GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, and GPT 5.6 as credited by Oum) and the formalisation run that used Claude Code; the older preprints' front matter and abstracts show no AI mention, but I did not read their full texts. The reading of the OpenAI claim as settled would rest on the expert endorsements and the Lean development; the reading of it as unsettled rests on the absence of refereeing, the unread PDF and the scope conflicts.
competing_reading: Read the OpenAI claim as established. The argument is two pages long; a named combinatorialist says it is correct; two named specialists have written expositions that reproduce each step; the Lean development has no sorry in any file I could read, and a second independent development reports sorry-free status. Three months without refereeing is normal for a 2026 preprint, and the attribution sentence (which I could not check against the PDF) would make the AI role load-bearing. On this reading the earlier withdrawn claims are irrelevant, because the formal check, not the record of earlier attempts, is what counts.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The text of OpenAI's proof and prompt PDFs, to confirm the statement, the attribution sentence and the 'at least 8 hours' prompt wording. (2) A build of openai/cdc-lean with lake, and the output of lake env lean CDCLean/Audit.lean showing only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, plus a grep for sorry across all files including any not listed. (3) A journal acceptance or a named referee report on the proof. (4) A specialist's check that the Lean statement (loopless multigraphs with Gamma = (ZMod 2)^3) matches the bullet's 'every bridgeless graph', including loops and multigraphs. (5) The first arXiv version of 2606.31134 that carries the CDC formalisation, and the Guo and Bajpai-Okur-Carmesin repositories. (6) A reading of Kintali's full paper and any response to it.
